newsitem.title: USA: Soft-spoken Herman wins new respect from UPS talks.
newsitem.headline: Soft-spoken Herman wins new respect from UPS talks.

text.p: In coaxing the Teamsters union and United Parcel Service back to the bargaining table, President Clinton's soft-spoken Labor Secretary Alexis Herman won new respect for her tenacity and skill.

The 49-year-old African American overcame race and sex barriers to win a coveted White House job and survived efforts to hold her Cabinet nomination hostage. She surprised skeptics by successfully prodding the two sides into ending the biggest labor dispute in two decades.
Both sides in the UPS strike made it clear that Herman played a pivotal role in achieving a settlement.
Ron Carey, Teamsters president, said, "I would like to thank Secretary of Labor Alexis Herman for all the hard work that she has put into this process."
And Dave Murray, chief negotiator for UPS, said, "A special thanks to her. She cleared her schedule, brought us here and hung in with us for five very difficult days and often sleepless nights."

With UPS talking impasse and the Teamsters accusing the country's major package carrier of intimidation and greed, Herman alone remained quietly optimistic that she could help breach the chasm dividing them.

"Alexis has had a history of people underestimating her," Joan Baggett, a labor official and former White House political director, told Business Week magazine recently. "She has a light touch, but she is very thorough."
Herman, a petite and elegant woman, persisted in her role of facilitator even after she had succeeded in bridging the bitterness that marked public exchanges between the union and the company.

While the two sides met day and night at a downtown hotel forging the deal that ended the 15-day strike, Herman refused to wait in her office three blocks away and took a room to be close at hand for consultation.

An ulterior motive may have been to apply subtle pressure on the negotiators. While not directly involved in the bargaining, Herman frequently applied gentle nudges to both sides to keep moving when enthusiasm flagged.
"Nobody's going to walk out on the secretary," a source close to the negotiations said.

Herman has been an inside player in Washington for many years. During the administration of President Jimmy Carter she set up and ran training programs in the South and headed the Labor Department's Women's Bureau.

Before Clinton was elected, she served on the Democratic National Committee where she worked closely with the late Commerce Secretary Ron Brown. She was chief executive officer of the 1992 Democratic Convention and she worked with the president on his transition team.
Most recently, Herman served as director of White House public liaison.
Her nomination to the Labor post was a battle right from the start. Three powerful interest groups within the Democratic Party each pushed their favorite candidate.
Labor unions wanted former Pennsylvania Sen. Harris Wofford to get the job, Hispanics lobbied for Rep. Estaban Torres of California.

But Herman, strongly backed by the National Organization for Women and civil rights activist Jesse Jackson -- for whom she worked during the 1988 presidential campaign -- won the day, only to have her nomination deadlocked for months by partisan political wrangling in the Senate.

Although Herman may not have been labor's candidate for the post, they soon rallied around the new secretary, noting her close relationship with Clinton and familiarity with internal White House politics as considerable pluses.
"Alexis Herman is a wonderful choice," AFL-CIO President John Sweeney said after her swearing-in.
Born in Mobile, Alabama, Herman is a graduate of Xavier University and began her career in 1969 as a social worker for Catholic Charities.
That led to her service in a black women's employment project in Atlanta and her apppointment in 1977 as director of the National Minority Women's Employment Program.
Herman is single and has no children.
